planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Coffea stenophylla tolerates considerably warmer lowland conditions than arabica and is best grown as a container specimen moved indoors for winter outside zones 10-12.

directions: Coffea stenophylla once supplied a modest nineteenth- and early twentieth-century export trade from Sierra Leone and parts of West Africa before falling out of cultivation by the 1920s in favor of robusta. Wild populations went largely unstudied until botanists from the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew rediscovered surviving trees in Sierra Leone, and subsequent cup tests found a sweet, complex flavor that trained tasters often mistook for high-quality arabica. Unlike arabica, it tolerates the hot lowland conditions and higher mean temperatures that suit robusta and liberica, making it a candidate parent for climate-resilient coffee breeding. Grow it as a small understory tree in humid, part-shaded, well-drained tropical soil, much like other wild Coffea species.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in deep, moisture-retentive, well-drained soil in partial shade; Excelsa coffee is a vigorous, deep-rooted tree that tolerates poor or peaty soils better than arabica and is best grown in a large container outside zones 10-12.

directions: First described in 1904 from Central Africa and long sold under the trade name Excelsa, this variety of liberica coffee grows as a vigorous, deep-rooted tree that tolerates poor, peaty, or seasonally flooded soils better than arabica or robusta. Its medium-sized, oval, lightly wrinkled beans brew a cup that is noticeably less bitter and less heavy than true liberica, with fruity, tart undertones that have made it a minor but persistent specialty crop in Vietnam and the Philippines. Recent genomic work has suggested it may merit recognition as a distinct species rather than a liberica variety, underscoring how little this plant has been studied compared with arabica and robusta. Site it in warm, humid, part-shaded conditions in deep, moisture-retentive soil, allowing ample room for its large tree form.
sources: Kew Royal Botanic Gardens — Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Tekisic Coffee is frost-tender and best grown as a container plant brought indoors for winter outside zones 10-11.

directions: Tekisic is a refined Bourbon selection developed in El Salvador through decades of mass selection carried out by the Salvadoran Institute of Coffee Research starting in the late 1940s; its name honors that institute's initials combined with a Nahuat word for work. Selected individuals were chosen for earlier ripening and higher yield than unimproved Bourbon at mid-to-high elevation, while retaining the dense, compact growth habit and strong cup quality that made the parent variety prized in the first place. It has since become one of the most widely planted coffee types in El Salvador, covering roughly half the country's coffee area. Grow and manage it like other Bourbon-type arabicas, under filtered shade in rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil.
sources: Instituto Salvadoreño de Investigaciones del Café (ISIC)

planting.note: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; IAPAR 59 is a compact, rust-resistant selection best grown as a container plant brought indoors for winter outside zones 10-11.

directions: IAPAR 59 was bred by Brazil's Instituto Agronômico do Paraná from a cross between the dwarf Villa Sarchi and the interspecific Híbrido de Timor, combining the Timor hybrid's broad leaf-rust resistance with Villa Sarchi's compact habit. It carries multiple resistance genes effective against essentially all known leaf-rust races, along with some tolerance to root-knot nematodes, making it valuable where rust pressure limits unimproved arabica. Its moderate stature suits closer spacing and mechanical harvesting, and the cultivar has also served as a parent in later rust-resistant releases. Cultivate it like other dwarf rust-resistant arabicas, in well-drained, slightly acidic soil under light shade.

planting.note: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Red Catuai is a compact, wind-tolerant selection best grown as a container plant brought indoors for winter outside zones 10-11.

directions: Catuaí was bred at Brazil's Instituto Agronômico de Campinas by crossing Mundo Novo with the compact Caturra, and the cross segregated into two still-grown color forms distinguished by ripe cherry color. The red-fruited form carries a noticeably thicker, sturdier stem than its yellow sibling and is generally considered to give a fuller-bodied, more fruit-forward cup, while sharing Catuaí's compact size, wind tolerance, and reliable bearing. Like other Catuaí selections it comes into production relatively quickly and performs well at closer spacing than taller heirloom varieties. Grow it under the same filtered shade and rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil used for other dwarf arabica cultivars.

planting.note: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Yellow Caturra is a scarce, compact color variant best grown as a container plant brought indoors for winter outside zones 10-11.

directions: Caturra itself arose as a natural compact mutant of Bourbon discovered in Brazil, and the yellow-fruited form is a further recessive color variant that ripens to gold rather than the usual red. It tends to ripen a little earlier than red Caturra and is often sought out by growers for its brighter, more citrus-forward acidity alongside Caturra's familiar cacao-toned sweetness. Because the yellow form appears only occasionally within Caturra populations, it remains a comparatively scarce specialty lot rather than a widely planted commercial type. Manage it like standard Caturra: a compact, high-density planting candidate that does best with good fertility and filtered shade at mid-to-high elevation.

planting.note: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; Catongo Cacao is a frost-tender tropical tree realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11.

directions: Catongo arose as a spontaneous albino mutation within Comum, the old Forastero-type landrace that has dominated Bahia, Brazil's cacao plantations since the crop's eighteenth-century introduction there, and it was identified and propagated by Bahian cacao researchers. The mutation removes anthocyanin pigment from both the beans and the flower's staminodes, giving white seeds and pale, ivory-colored staminodes instead of the usual purple tones. Chocolate made from Catongo beans is prized in the fine-flavor market for being less astringent and bitter than standard bulk cacao, with a lighter color and caramel-leaning notes. Grow it under the same high humidity, filtered shade, and rich, moist soil required by other Forastero-type cacao.

planting.note: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; Pound 7 is a frost-tender tropical tree realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11.

directions: Pound 7 is an Upper Amazon Forastero clone collected by Trinidad agronomist F.J. Pound during a 1930s expedition into the Loreto region of Peru in search of cacao genetic diversity. Brought back to Trinidad's cacao germplasm collection, it became one of the historically important Upper Amazon parent types used alongside the ICS clones in twentieth-century Trinidadian hybrid breeding programs. It remains a reference genotype in contemporary cacao genetics research, valued for representing both wild Amazonian diversity and the pedigree behind many modern hybrids. Cultivate it as a grafted or rooted-cutting tree under filtered shade in rich, moist, well-drained tropical soil.
sources: International Cocoa Genebank, Trinidad (University of the West Indies)

planting.note: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; UF 667 is a frost-tender tropical tree realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11.

directions: UF 667 is a Trinitario-type clone from the historic cacao-growing region of Bahia, Brazil, maintained as part of the collections Brazilian breeding programs have drawn on to develop improved biclonal hybrid planting stock for local farmers. It is notable among Bahia germplasm for carrying a red-pod trait that has been passed on to some of the hybrid cultivars bred from it. As with other Trinitario selections, its ancestry blends Criollo and Forastero traits, giving it value as a breeding parent even though it is not typically grown as a standalone commercial variety. Grow grafted material under filtered shade in rich, moist, well-drained soil like other cacao selections.
sources: Comissão Executiva do Plano da Lavoura Cacaueira (CEPLAC)

planting.note: Train stem cuttings onto rough-barked trees, cork slabs, or a shaded trellis in partial shade with high humidity and moist, well-drained organic medium; Vanilla africana is a West African climbing orchid grown mainly as a botanical specimen rather than for pod production.

directions: Vanilla africana is a succulent-stemmed climbing orchid native to the forests of West Tropical Africa east to Gabon, where it scrambles over trees and shrubs from sea level up to about 3,000 feet using aerial roots produced at each stem node. Its fragrant white or pale yellow flowers carry purplish markings on the lip, a pattern shared with several related African Vanilla species. It has never been developed into a cultivated vanilla-bean crop and is grown almost exclusively as a botanical curiosity rather than for pod production. Train it onto rough bark or a humid, shaded support much like other climbing Vanilla species, in a loose, fast-draining organic medium.
sources: Kew Royal Botanic Gardens — Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Mount young plants on rough-barked trees, cork slabs, or a shaded trellis in partial shade with high humidity and a coarse, fast-draining epiphytic medium; Vanilla madagascariensis is a Madagascar-endemic climbing orchid grown mainly for its showy flowers rather than for pod production.

directions: Vanilla madagascariensis is endemic to Madagascar, where it grows as a large epiphyte with a thick, smooth, green climbing stem in humid evergreen forest and drier coastal forest along the island's east, up to roughly 2,600 feet. It produces large, showy white flowers with a pink-to-apricot throat on the lip over a long fall-through-spring bloom season, closely resembling the related Vanilla phalaenopsis of the Seychelles and Vanilla roscheri of East Africa, though it differs from both in details of lip shape. Unlike Vanilla planifolia, it is not grown for pod production and is cultivated mainly by orchid specialists for its flowers. Mount it on rough bark or a humid, shaded support in a coarse, fast-draining epiphytic mix.
sources: Kew Royal Botanic Gardens — Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Train stem cuttings onto rough-barked trees, cork slabs, or a shaded trellis in partial shade with high humidity and moist, well-drained organic medium; Vanilla chamissonis is a South American climbing orchid assessed as endangered, so source only nursery-propagated material.

directions: Vanilla chamissonis is a wide-ranging South American vanilla species found from French Guiana south through Brazil's Atlantic Forest to Bolivia and northeastern Argentina, where it grows as a long, nomadic climbing vine rooting both in soil and onto bark as it ascends. Unlike most Vanilla species, which trick pollinators with no reward, its flowers offer a genuine nectar reward to the euglossine bees that pollinate it, a trait that has drawn particular interest from orchid researchers. It blooms in the southern-hemisphere summer with fruit ripening roughly a year and a half later, but ongoing habitat loss in the Atlantic Forest has left it assessed as endangered. Grow it on rough bark or a shaded trellis in humid, warm conditions with a fast-draining organic medium, sourcing only nursery-propagated stock.
sources: Kew Royal Botanic Gardens — Plants of the World Online
IUCN Red List of Threatened Species

planting.note: Train stem cuttings onto rough-barked trees, cork slabs, or a shaded trellis in partial shade with a fast-draining organic medium and a drier seasonal rest period; Vanilla polylepis is native to seasonally dry African woodland rather than rainforest.

directions: Vanilla polylepis is a climbing orchid native to seasonally dry woodland and thicket from Kenya south through Tanzania, Malawi, Zambia, Zimbabwe, and Angola, a markedly drier habitat than the rainforest settings favored by most cultivated Vanilla species. It is grown almost entirely as a botanical and conservation subject rather than for pod production. Its tolerance of seasonal dryness has made it of interest to researchers screening wild Vanilla relatives for traits, such as drought and disease tolerance, that might be bred into commercial vanilla. Train it onto rough bark or a shaded support in a fast-draining medium, allowing a drier rest period that mimics its native dry-season climate.
sources: Kew Royal Botanic Gardens — Plants of the World Online
